subject: data-science
question: Does p = 0.03 mean there is a 3% chance that the new checkout has no effect?

artifact.result: A/B test of a new checkout: two-sided test, p = 0.03

ai_claim: Yes. The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true, so there is a 3% chance of no effect and a 97% chance the effect is real.

ai_solution.text: The null hypothesis is that the checkout has no effect.
The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
So there is a 97% chance the effect is real.

failure.misconception: Reading a p-value as the probability of the hypothesis
failure.explanation: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true: P(data | H0), not P(H0 | data). It says nothing directly about the chance the effect is real, which also depends on prior plausibility and power. p = 0.03 means results like these would be fairly unusual under no effect.
failure.why_convincing: The misreading sounds like what a p-value ought to mean, and it is extremely common.

canonical_solution: No: p = 0.03 is the probability of data this extreme assuming no effect, not the probability that there is no effect.

valid_evidence.summary: The p-value is P(result at least this extreme | H0) = 0.03.
With a very implausible hypothesis and a low-powered test, many results with p = 0.03 are false positives.

counterexamples: P(data | H0) and P(H0 | data) can differ greatly, just as P(wet | rain) differs from P(rain | wet).

hints.text: Recall the conditional probability a p-value represents.
Step 3 states what the p-value is.
A p-value conditions on the null hypothesis being true.
Compare P(data | H0) with P(H0 | data).
Step 3 is wrong: p is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data).

repair: Report: 'If there were no effect, a difference this large would occur about 3% of the time.'
debrief: The p-value is one of the most misread numbers in science. Say what it conditions on, and add effect sizes and intervals rather than turning p into a probability of truth.

subject: data-science
question: Is the conclusion justified?

artifact.analysis:
After a UI change, the team tested 20 metrics, each at a 0.05 significance level.
One metric (time on settings page) was significant: p = 0.04. The other 19 were not.
artifact.conclusion: "The UI change significantly increased time on the settings page."

ai_claim: Yes. The settings-page metric was significant at p = 0.04, below the 0.05 threshold, so the effect is real.

ai_solution.text: 0.04 is below 0.05, so it is significant.
So the UI change increased time on the settings page.

failure.explanation: With 20 independent tests at 0.05, about one false positive is expected even with no real effects (1 - 0.95^20 = 64% chance of at least one). One significant result out of 20 is exactly what chance produces. Correct for multiplicity (e.g. Bonferroni: 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025, which 0.04 does not meet) or pre-register a primary metric.
failure.why_convincing: Each test on its own is computed correctly.

canonical_solution: No: one 'hit' in 20 tests is expected by chance. After a Bonferroni correction the threshold is 0.0025, and p = 0.04 is not significant.

valid_evidence.summary: Bonferroni threshold: 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025, and p = 0.04 is above it.

counterexamples: Running 20 tests on two identical versions typically yields one 'significant' metric.

hints.text: Ask how many tests were run.
Step 3 applies the single-test threshold.
The chance of a false positive grows with the number of tests.
Compute 1 - 0.95^20.
Step 3 is wrong: with 20 tests, one p < 0.05 is expected by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons.

repair: Pre-register a primary metric, and correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni or FDR).
debrief: The more you test, the more 'significant' results you find by luck. Count the tests before trusting any single one.

subject: data-science
question: If a transaction is flagged, what is the probability, in percent, that it is actually fraudulent?

artifact.test: Fraud screen: flags 99% of fraudulent transactions (sensitivity), and wrongly flags 5% of legitimate ones (false positive rate).

ai_claim: 99. The screen catches 99% of fraud, so a flagged transaction is 99% likely to be fraud.

ai_solution.text: A flag therefore indicates fraud 99% of the time.
The false positive rate is small, only 5%.
So a flagged transaction is 99% likely to be fraud.

failure.misconception: Confusing P(flag | fraud) with P(fraud | flag)
failure.explanation: Out of 10,000 transactions, 100 are fraud and 99 of them are flagged. Of the 9,900 legitimate ones, 5% - 495 - are also flagged. So 99 of 594 flags are fraud: about 16.7%. Because fraud is rare, false positives outnumber true positives. This is the base rate fallacy.
failure.why_convincing: 99% is the most prominent number, and 5% sounds small.

valid_evidence.summary: Only 1% of transactions are fraud, so legitimate transactions dominate the flags.

counterexamples: Most flagged transactions, about 83%, are legitimate.

hints.text: Work with 10,000 transactions.
Step 2 reverses the conditional probability.
Bayes' theorem: P(fraud | flag) depends on the base rate.
Count true flags and false flags.
Step 2 is wrong: only about 16.7% of flags are fraud, because fraud is rare.

debrief: With rare events, even accurate tests produce mostly false alarms. Always combine sensitivity and false positive rate with the base rate before interpreting a positive.

transfer_check.question: With the same screen, if 10% of transactions were fraudulent, what percent of flags would be fraud?

subject: data-science
question: Is the report's interpretation of the interval correct?

artifact.result: Mean delivery time from a sample of 400 deliveries: 30 minutes, 95% CI [28, 32]
artifact.report: "95% of deliveries take between 28 and 32 minutes."

ai_claim: Yes. The 95% confidence interval is 28 to 32 minutes, so 95% of deliveries take between 28 and 32 minutes.

ai_solution.text: A 95% interval contains 95% of the values.

failure.misconception: Treating a confidence interval for the mean as a range for individual values
failure.explanation: The interval describes uncertainty about the average delivery time, not the spread of individual deliveries. With n = 400, the standard error is SD / 20, so a CI of +-2 minutes implies an SD of about 10 minutes: individual deliveries range far wider, roughly 10 to 50 minutes. A prediction interval or percentiles describe individual deliveries.

canonical_solution: No: the CI covers the mean, not individual deliveries. With SD about 10 minutes, individual times vary far more widely.

valid_evidence.summary: Half-width 2 = 1.96 x SD / sqrt(400) gives SD = 2 x 20 / 1.96 = about 10.2 minutes.
Many single deliveries take 45 minutes, far outside [28, 32].

counterexamples: An individual delivery of 45 minutes is normal given an SD of about 10.

hints.text: Ask what quantity the interval is about.
Step 3 applies the interval to individual deliveries.
A CI for the mean shrinks with sample size; the spread of individual values does not.
Back out the standard deviation from the interval's width.
Step 3 is wrong: the CI is for the mean. Individual deliveries vary far more.

repair: Report the mean with its CI, and describe individual deliveries with percentiles (e.g. 90% take under 45 minutes).
debrief: Confidence intervals for a mean narrow as samples grow; the variability of individuals does not. Say which one you are reporting.
